intro: The total-market title fight: Vanguard's flagship versus Fidelity's free upstart. Same job — own the entire US stock market — with the difference coming down to four basis points, a $3,000 minimum, and one quiet string attached.
verdict: In an IRA or 401(k), FZROX's zero fee and zero minimum make it the marginal winner. In a taxable account, VTSAX's portability (FZROX can't transfer in kind out of Fidelity) is worth far more than four basis points. Either way you'll retire within rounding error of the same number.

intro: Vanguard versus Schwab for total-market supremacy. Both track essentially the entire US stock market; the gap is one basis point of fee and the brand on the statement.
verdict: Hold whichever lives at your brokerage. SWTSX is a basis point cheaper with no minimum; VTSAX has Vanguard's index pedigree and quarterly distributions. Paying a transaction fee to switch between them would be the only real mistake available here.

intro: Vanguard's total-market fund against Fidelity's. The two are so similar that the comparison is mostly a Rorschach test for which brand you already trust.
verdict: FSKAX is cheaper (0.015% vs 0.04%) with no minimum, making it the better standalone pick — but the funds are functionally identical and the choice should follow your account location, not a basis-point spreadsheet.

intro: The classic Vanguard family argument: total market or just the S&P 500? Same firm, same fee, same minimum — the only real difference is whether you want the smaller 20% of the US market that VFIAX leaves out.
verdict: A coin flip dressed as a decision. VTSAX adds mid and small caps for the same 0.04%; VFIAX is the purer blue-chip benchmark. Their long-run returns track closely. Pick one, never hold both expecting diversification, and stop comparing them.

intro: Two S&P 500 funds from the two biggest names in indexing. Identical 500 stocks, near-identical returns; the contest is fee and minimum.
verdict: FXAIX edges it on paper — 0.015% versus 0.04%, no minimum versus $3,000 — but both are so cheap the difference is lunch money per year. Your brokerage decides this one.

intro: Fidelity versus Schwab in the race to the cheapest S&P 500 fund. We're now arguing over fractions of a basis point, which tells you the war is essentially over and investors won.
verdict: SWPPX (0.02%) and FXAIX (0.015%) are interchangeable. The 'better' fund is whichever your money already sits next to. Genuinely — flip a coin and go fund your account.

intro: An all-Fidelity question: the zero-fee total market fund, or the near-zero S&P 500 fund? It's really two questions — total market vs. large-cap, and free-but-trapped vs. cheap-but-portable.
verdict: FZROX owns the whole market for free but can't leave Fidelity in kind; FXAIX is the S&P 500 for 0.015% and travels. In an IRA, FZROX. In taxable, FXAIX (or an ETF). The total-market-vs-500 difference matters more than the fee.

intro: Fidelity's own total-market civil war: the free proprietary-index fund against the 0.015% Dow-Jones-tracking one. The entire decision hinges on one feature most people never use — portability.
verdict: IRA money: FZROX, because free beats 0.015% and you'd sell to move anyway. Taxable money: FSKAX, because it can transfer in kind to another broker without triggering a tax bill. The performance difference is statistical noise.

intro: Vanguard's S&P 500 Admiral shares versus Schwab's. The index is identical by definition; the fight is fee, minimum, and house loyalty.
verdict: SWPPX wins the spec sheet — 0.02% and no minimum against 0.04% and $3,000 — but VFIAX carries the lineage of the original index fund. At these fees, account location is the only tiebreaker that matters.

intro: Total international, paid versus free. Vanguard's 0.09% all-cap fund against Fidelity's zero-fee version — with the usual ZERO-fund catch and one coverage gap.
verdict: FZILX is free but Fidelity-locked and skips international small caps; VTIAX costs 0.09%, includes small caps, and travels. IRA at Fidelity: FZILX is fine. Want completeness and portability: VTIAX. The bigger decision is owning international at all.

intro: The two heavyweight total-international index funds. Both span developed and emerging markets including small caps; remarkably, Fidelity's is the cheaper one.
verdict: FTIHX (0.06%, no minimum) narrowly beats VTIAX (0.09%, $3,000) on cost and coverage is equivalent. A genuine near-tie — let your brokerage break it. Either gives you the whole world outside the US in one line.

intro: Total international versus developed-markets-only. This isn't a fee fight — it's a coverage decision, because SWISX deliberately excludes emerging markets (and Canada).
verdict: VTIAX is the more complete one-fund answer, including emerging markets and small caps. SWISX suits investors who want developed markets only or size EM separately. Know what you're buying: these track different slices of the world, not the same slice at different prices.

intro: The two default total-bond funds, both tracking the Bloomberg US Aggregate. Bonds are even more commoditized than stocks, so this is about as close as fund comparisons get.
verdict: FXNAX is cheaper (0.025% vs 0.05%) with no minimum, giving it a hair's edge — but they hold the same index with the same behavior. Account location decides it. Spend your energy on the stock/bond ratio instead, which is the only bond decision that moves outcomes.

intro: Vanguard versus Schwab for the boring, essential bond slot. Same Aggregate index, fee difference of a single basis point.
verdict: SWAGX (0.04%) and VBTLX (0.05%) are the same fund in different wrappers. Hold whichever your brokerage offers without a transaction fee, keep it in a tax-advantaged account, and move on.

intro: Own the whole world, or just the US? VTWAX holds every stock on earth at market weight; VTSAX holds only the United States. This is a real allocation decision wearing a fund-comparison costume.
verdict: VTWAX is maximum simplicity — one fund, global, never rebalanced by region — at 0.10%. VTSAX is cheaper and US-only, a deliberate home-country bet. Neither is wrong; just don't mistake the all-US fund for a globally diversified one.

intro: One of the strongest active records in history against the index it's measured by. Will Danoff's Contrafund versus a plain S&P 500 fund — the active-vs-passive debate in its most credible form.
verdict: Contrafund's long-term record under Danoff genuinely beat the index, and its fee was long a bargain — though Fidelity's performance-based pricing has since pushed it to around 0.74%. But recent results have been mixed, succession is an open question, and FXAIX costs a fraction. Respect the record; the index is still the percentage play, especially for new money.

intro: The advisor channel's flagship growth fund versus a Vanguard S&P 500 fund. The comparison is incomplete without one number AGTHX's chart hides: the sales load.
verdict: Load-waived (in a 401(k)), AGTHX is a decent active growth fund competing fairly on its 0.58% fee. Load-paid, the up-to-5.75% front commission means you start nearly 6% behind VFIAX before the manager does anything. Check your share class; the answer flips entirely on it.

intro: T. Rowe's celebrated Blue Chip Growth fund against Vanguard's growth index. Both bet on the same mega-cap growth names; one charges twenty times more to do it.
verdict: TRBCX dazzled through the 2010s, then fell far harder than VIGAX in 2022 — the honest shape of concentrated active growth. At 0.70% vs 0.05%, you're paying for concentration that helps and hurts in roughly equal measure. The index is the lower-variance, lower-cost default.

intro: Two of the best balanced funds ever run, head to head — David Giroux's (largely closed) Capital Appreciation against Vanguard's 95-year-old Wellington.
verdict: Both are rare active funds worth the fee. PRWCX has the more spectacular recent record but is mostly closed to new investors and rests on one manager; VWELX is open, institutionally durable, and cheaper at 0.26%. If you can't get PRWCX (most can't), VWELX is no consolation prize.

intro: The Wellington siblings. Same manager (Wellington Management), same firm, opposite temperaments: one leans stocks, the other leans bonds. The choice is really about your stomach.
verdict: VWELX (~65% stocks) is for growth-with-ballast; VWINX (~35% stocks) is for capital preservation and income. Younger or more aggressive: Wellington. Near or in retirement, allergic to drawdowns: Wellesley. Both are among the few active funds this site recommends without wincing.

intro: Active deep value against indexed value. Dodge & Cox's honorable, committee-run stock fund versus Vanguard's brainless large-value index — the rare active/passive matchup that's genuinely close.
verdict: DODGX is the active fund to own if you own any, with shareholder-aligned structure and a real after-fee record. But VVIAX delivers the value style for 0.05% versus 0.51%, and over full cycles the index keeps the race close. Conviction in the strategy justifies DODGX; default rationality justifies VVIAX.

intro: The 2040 target-date showdown: Vanguard versus Fidelity's index series. Both are all-index, one-fund retirement portfolios for roughly the same retirement year.
verdict: VFORX (0.08%) is a touch cheaper than FBIFX (0.12%); glide paths and international weights differ slightly. Both are excellent. Pick the one matching your brokerage — and if you're at Fidelity, triple-check the word 'Index' is in the name, since the active Freedom twin costs several times more.

intro: 2050 target-date funds from Vanguard and Schwab, both all-index, both built to be your entire retirement account.
verdict: A dead heat at 0.08% each, with minor glide-path differences. SWYMX's $1 minimum is friendlier for absolute beginners; VFIFX has Vanguard's longer target-date track record. Account location wins. The real value of either is the behavior it enforces, not the basis points.

intro: Two ways to invest in retirement: Vanguard's all-index Target Retirement Income fund against the actively managed Wellesley Income. Similar conservative temperaments, different engines.
verdict: VTINX is cheaper (0.08%), all-index, includes a TIPS sleeve and international exposure, and rebalances on a fixed schedule. VWINX (0.23%) is active, US-focused, with a longer record and slightly higher equity. For pure cost and diversification, VTINX; for those who specifically trust Wellington's hand, Wellesley.

intro: Indexed growth against one of Fidelity's aggressive active growth funds. Same mega-cap-growth neighborhood; wildly different fee and volatility profiles.
verdict: FBGRX swings harder than VIGAX in both directions and has a competitive long-term record, but at 0.72% vs 0.05% it must consistently out-pick the index to justify itself. As a contained satellite for someone who understands the volatility, defensible. As a core growth holding, VIGAX is the cheaper, calmer default.

intro: Small-cap indexing, Vanguard versus Fidelity — with a subtle index difference (CRSP vs Russell 2000) that has historically nudged returns.
verdict: Near-identical on cost (0.05% vs 0.025%). VSMAX's CRSP index runs slightly larger and has historically edged the Russell 2000 that FSSNX tracks, owing to the Russell's mechanical June reconstitution. A small lean toward VSMAX in a vacuum; let your brokerage decide in practice.

intro: Mid-cap index funds from Vanguard and Fidelity. The market's quiet overachiever segment, tracked by two near-identical low-cost funds.
verdict: FSMDX (0.025%, Russell Midcap, no minimum) is marginally cheaper than VIMAX (0.05%, CRSP Mid Cap, $3,000). Both do the one job cleanly. The index methodologies differ slightly but outcomes converge. Brokerage location is the deciding vote.

intro: Active bond royalty against the passive default. PIMCO Total Return — once the largest fund on earth — versus a plain total-bond index fund.
verdict: PTTRX's post-Gross team has quietly beaten the Agg in most recent years, and bonds are active management's least-bad arena. But the famous 0.51% institutional fee requires institutional access, retail classes cost more, and the core-plus complexity adds risk. VBTLX at 0.05% is the simpler, sufficient core. Plausible active edge; never a necessity.

intro: Two of the most respected active bond funds, with very different risk dials. PIMCO Income reaches for yield through credit and mortgages; Dodge & Cox Income is a more measured core-plus fund.
verdict: PIMIX has the higher yield and the standout long-term record — but it's a credit-risk fund that falls in risk-off panics. DODIX is steadier and cheaper (0.41% vs 0.51%), closer to a true core holding. For a yield satellite, PIMIX; for the dependable bond anchor, DODIX. Don't confuse the two roles.

intro: Developed-international index funds, Fidelity versus Vanguard. Both skip emerging markets; the wrinkle is small-cap coverage and a one-basis-point fee gap.
verdict: FSPSX (0.035%, MSCI EAFE, large/mid only) is cheaper; VTMGX (0.08%) adds developed small caps for slightly more. The coverage difference is minor and the cost difference is trivial. As ever, hold the one your brokerage offers without friction.
